title: Buddhisms Two Truths Q&A
speaker: Jason Ruvelson
summary: Jason Ruvelson answers questions on the two truths, starting with ultimate reality and how understanding of it keeps coming into question the further study goes. Emptiness and dharmakaya, which Jason calls the fabric of space, cannot be separated from form or relative reality, since arising and the people sitting in the room are part of what is there. Jason then describes the three jewels of Buddha, Dharma and Sangha, including the historical Buddha, Buddha nature, and the tea and study shared in the Bellingham Dharma hall. When a participant says Sangha means the community of the enlightened, Jason answers that it can include the lineage, the local group, all humans, and all beings seen and unseen. Indra's net comes up as the exchange closes.

sentences.text: Those of you who are staying, if there are any questions, maybe we can come back together for a minute.
Question?
Yeah?
Ultimate reality is interesting because one thing about Buddhism in general is you study something and you eventually gain some kind of understanding about what it is.
Then as time goes on, you realize you don't understand, and you go further into it.
I realized even in preparing for this talk that that experience was very alive for me.
It's like, "Oh, yeah, of course I can talk about ultimate reality."
And then I get into it more and more and my own understanding starts to come into question.
One of the things that came up for me in studying it was that we often talk about emptiness as being ultimate reality.
Emptiness, they might say, dharmakaya, which is basically like a metaphor, the fabric of space or pregnant space.
So that's dharmakaya.
But when you talk about ultimate reality, you can't talk about it separate from form.
You also can't talk about it separate from relative reality, because it's not like all there is is emptiness and space.
There's also arising.
There's also us here, sitting here.
It just may not be quite as solid as we think it is.
Again, there are different kinds of emptiness.
There's emptiness of self, and there's emptiness of self and other, or emptiness of other.
And dharmakaya, I guess, is speaking to all of that.
But the danger here is intellectualizing this stuff too much, and any time you talk about it, it's hard not to go there.
That's why it's so important to practice, because everything we're talking about isn't some kind of intellectual understanding.
It's an actual experience.
But these teachings help point that out to us, to see when we're fooling ourselves and getting caught and so on.
Yes, very much.
Yes, to say about that.
Well, it's interesting, because in doing this talk, I realized I can't speak for all of Buddhism.
I can speak for what I know, which is of this lineage and tradition.
I realized some things are very similar and maybe identical, and other things may be very different.
The one thing that I think is true of all Buddhism is the three jewels of Buddha, Dharma and Sangha: that we value them all equally and profoundly.
The Sangha being community, we're going to practice together, our community acts as mirrors for us, we support each other, and it illuminates ourselves.
And Dharma: teachings, the truth of how things are, but also Buddhist teachings.
There are many kinds of Buddhist teachings.
There are some that are more psychological and some that go further into emptiness, and so on and so on.
And also the notion of Buddha.
Buddha has various levels to it.
Buddha being the historical Buddha, someone who started this lineage and began these teachings.
Buddha also as inherent nature, the Buddha nature, basic goodness.
It's something within ourselves, all of us.
The historical Buddha was a human being just like us and exemplified that same potential that we have.
Sorry, I expanded on Sangha a little bit.
Yeah, actually, more about Sangha: it's fun to practice together.
It's one of the great things here in Bellingham.
We have this Dharma hall and people come together and practice.
I know in our group we definitely have fun practicing together and having tea and chatting and studying together, and I'm sure it's the same in other groups.
It's a big part of Buddhism in general.
Other questions?
Anything?
Yeah.
**Participant:** I think that Sangha refers to the community of the enlightened.
To say you're arhats, and it makes sense.
If you're really talking about the three jewels, and they're the equivalent of what you're talking about, one being Buddha.
Well, it seems to me that the general community can be very confused.
So to play it as a jewel might be a little misleading.
And then to have some sense that the Sangha actually refers to...
**Jason Ruvelson:** Again, I think Sangha is spoken of on different levels.
I think, sure, Sangha could be those enlightened beings that have gone before us.
They're part of the lineage that brought the teachings here to us.
They're also our local community of people that practice together, that support us in our own practice.
And I also think they could be considered all human beings on the planet.
For that matter, all beings in the universe, seen and unseen.
If you say Sangha, by definition, is those enlightened beings, well, that's something we all have, by nature.
Maybe it's not recognized right now.
So I think to pin Sangha down to one group and not another...
Indra's net?
Did you say Indra's net?
What did you say?
Indra's net.
Is that what Trungpa Rinpoche?
Another question.
Yeah.
